chapter: Faking parts and the Tuxedo bands
title: Dutcher asks how Dixieland trombone is played; most played by ear
summary: Dutcher asks what a trombonist thinks about when improvising. Ridgley says old trombonists were mostly a gift and played by ear, naming those who could and could not read.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: The question, Risley, I've had this formal education in playing trombone in concert bands, in marching bands. But I'm always playing set notes of music, something that somebody else has written for me. And I'm very enchanted by this Dixieland music where the trombone player seems to be making it up and improvising and playing things that aren't written. And the music is a very happy type of music, which I think is good for relaxation for lawyers, among other people. And I'm wondering, how do you play, what do you think of when you play this Dixieland music?

Well, at our time back there, you know, we wasn't much of a reader. Spellers, and the trombone, he didn't do much. Most of the time he had bass licks, you know. And then he had nod, then he'd have a little solo or something. But he didn't play trombone like those fellas. The most was a gift, and we done most sliding and faking on such an audible step, you see. We couldn't play no trombone like those boys were playing that they didn't know how. You see, and which was just mostly a gift. And most of us played from ear on trombone. There wasn't many of the, Ory wasn't a reader, Jack Carey wasn't a reader, I was a little bit better reading what they were, but not much. And many of the other trombone, Frankie Dusen didn't read, and Willie Connish didn't read. And most of the trombone, Buddy Johnson, he was a reader, a little bit, but his brother Yank didn't read. Vic Jasper was a reader, you see, and trombone
